newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Stormy weather frazzles Argentine cotton sowing.
newsitem.headline: Stormy weather frazzles Argentine cotton sowing.

text.p: Argentina's cotton farmers have been battered by wet and windy, unusually cool weather which has dampened early season hopes of a bumper harvest, a top cotton exporter said.

After a winter drought, October rains brought soil moisture to good levels for sowing an area approaching last season's one million hectares. But it kept on raining, forcing some farmers to resow in the center of key Chaco province.
Brusque temperature changes and winds have also hampered late sowing and damaged immature plants, Rafael Almiroty of Almiroty y Compania told Reuters.
"The cotton belt has been suffering from the savagery of the weather," he said.
But he said that dry weather for the next few weeks could still allow sowing to be completed and damage to be reversed.

"It is still not too alarming. The climatic problems can still be overcome if the weather allows producers to finish the rest of the sowing and and resow what they have to," he said, "By January we will have a good idea of how things are likely to turn out."
January, when the cotton flowers, is the crucial month for the plants' development. Too much moisture now could stunt root development and leave it vulnerable to future dry spells.
The very latest sowing must normally be completed by the first week of January.
In October, Almiroty had predicted another big cotton season for Argentina, with between 900,000 hectares and one million hectares planted.
The government's Agriculture Secretariat said on Thursday that 71.2 percent of an intended sowing area of 989,000 hectares had been planted by December 6.

Farmers planted a record one million hectares in 1995/96, with final output totaling 425,000 tonnes of lint, according to Almiroty. This was up from sown area of 700,000 hectares the previous season and from just 300,000 to 400,000 hectares in most recent years.
Most of Argentina's cotton is exported, with the troubled local textile industry taking about 100,000 tonnes of lint.
